SRC_1: In 1874, six men set off into Colorado’s San Juan Mountains in winter hoping to reach newly discovered goldfields on the other side.
Two months later, only one man emerged from the mountains, and he looked weirdly fed instead of emaciated.
The man was Alfred Packer, also known as the Colorado Cannibal.
On the morning of April 16, 1874, men at Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado saw a distressed man enter their mess hall during a snowstorm.
The man who entered the mess hall was Alfred Packer.
Alfred had rags on his feet, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging from a strap on one side, and a rifle on the other.
General Charles Adams oversaw the agency and had his men help Alfred to a table with food.
Alfred ate so quickly that he threw up.
After several whiskeys, Alfred told the agency men about his journey over the mountains.
Alfred said the others with him had become too exhausted to continue, that he had gotten snow blindness and frostbite, and that he had been left behind to fend for himself.
Alfred said that for months he had eaten rabbits, roots, and rosebuds, and that his experience as a guide got him out alive.
Several months earlier, on November 20, 1873, the party Alfred eventually joined set out from Bingham Canyon in Utah as part of a group of 20.
The travelers were heading to newly found goldfields near Breckenridge in Colorado.
The group met Alfred about 25 miles south of Salt Lake City when they bumped into him during the journey.
Alfred offered his services and claimed he was a guide who knew the territory between Utah and Brackenridge well.
The group agreed to take Alfred with them because they thought a guide would help them.
Alfred actually had no idea where he was going, and he had only worked as a guide for a few months.
As a guide, Alfred often got lost and tended to argue with clients.
Alfred had a reputation for stealing and lying.
When he was younger, Alfred served twice in the Union Army during the Civil War.
Each of Alfred’s Army enlistments lasted only a few months because he had epilepsy and was prone to seizures.
Alfred was honorably discharged both times from the Union Army.
After his discharges, Alfred worked driving horses and other draft animals across the West.
Alfred also worked as a hunter, a range hand, and an odd-job worker for mining companies.
Alfred tried mining in Colorado, but these jobs did not last long because he had a bad attitude and kept getting fired.
By the time the expedition reached just outside Montrose, Alfred had gotten them there only by luck.
The route from Utah to Colorado was slowed by heavy snow, making it almost impossible to follow the trail.
By January, the party was out of food and had begun eating horse feed and considering eating the horses.
The men later described Alfred as greedy, lazy, and constantly fighting with someone.
On January 21, the party stumbled across a Ute camp led by Chief Ouray in a valley just outside Montrose.
Chief Ouray gave the men food and shelter and suggested that they stay until the weather improved.
The party still had roughly 120 miles and the San Juan Mountains left to cross.
Chief Ouray warned them that no Ute would attempt the journey in those conditions and that it would mean certain death.
The safest option, according to Chief Ouray, was to wait out the winter.
The men worried that other groups would reach the gold before they did.
The party decided to split in two, leaving half behind with the horses and wagons until spring while the other half tried to reach Los Piños Indian Agency.
Chief Ouray gave directions for the route he thought best, telling them to drop down to the Gunnison River and follow it before heading north to the agency.
Alfred insisted it would be better to cross the mountains directly because he claimed it was much quicker and he knew the area.
Five of the men believed Alfred and went with him.
The other group followed the river with food from Chief Ouray.
The river journey was brutal, and the food ran out before the men reached the agency.
Cowhands working in the area found the starving men and fed them at their cattle camp until spring.
The four men who stayed with the river party reached the agency in April and got there in May.
When those men arrived, Alfred had already been there and left, and none of the others had come with him.
According to the expedition leader, after leaving the Ute camp Alfred’s party followed the river on horseback until the horses could go no farther.
The leader then unloaded the provisions and walked the horses back to the Ute camp.
It is thought that the party walked a bit farther down the river and then took a path high into the mountains.
When the leader left them, he knew they did not have enough supplies to reach the agency.
After being left, the men had only about 14 days of food.
The men also lacked adequate clothing, snowshoes, flints, and hardly any matches.
Their only weapons were a few rifles, one pistol, a hatchet, and some knives.
No one heard from the men again until Alfred appeared at the agency months later.
When Alfred arrived at the agency, he looked unusually well-fed for a starving man.
Alfred went to Saguache after feeling better and rented a room and a saloon.
In Saguache, Alfred spent over $100 on drinking and gambling, which the narration equates to about $3,800 in 2023.
Alfred also spent another $78 in the general store.
People reported that Alfred often gave conflicting stories about what happened when he drank.
Some people said Alfred seemed to use a different wallet every time he went out and never ran out of cash.
Alfred had sold his rifle at the agency for $10, and that sale did not explain the rest of his money.
Preston Nutter was the man who arrived at the agency in May and led the other party that followed the river.
Preston went to Saguache to look for answers after leaving the agency.
Preston immediately suspected Alfred’s story because he already knew Alfred was a liar.
Preston told General Adams that the other men would not have left Alfred for dead.
Preston said the rifle Alfred sold belonged to an old man in the group and that the pipe Alfred left behind belonged to Shannon Bell.
Preston also pointed out that Alfred had had no money when he originally joined the group.
General Adams sent a man on horseback to bring Alfred in for questioning.
When Alfred returned, Adams and his men asked where he had gotten the money, why he had other men’s belongings, and how he had survived the mountains while appearing well-fed.
Alfred first claimed that his feet got wet and cold, so he stayed by the fire while the others went for food and then never returned.
Preston rejected that account because the others were prospectors and Alfred had still been the better option than no guide.
A council was formed to investigate what happened.
Two members of the Ute tribe then arrived at the agency with pieces of flesh they said came from a human found on a hill near the agency.
When he saw the flesh, Alfred panicked, fainted, woke up, begged for mercy, and then gave a different story.
Alfred reportedly said, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry.”
Alfred then said the party ran out of food ten days into the journey.
Alfred said the oldest man died first, and the others ate him and took his rifle.
Alfred said another man died five days later, and the others ate him too and found $133 in his pockets.
Alfred said another man died after that while Alfred was away getting wood for the fire, and the remaining men ate him too.
Alfred said Shannon Bell then shot the remaining men.
Alfred said he and Shannon carried some of the bodies’ meat with them for food and covered up the rest.
Alfred said Shannon later tried to kill him two weeks afterward.
Alfred said he shot Shannon in self-defense when Shannon went mad and attacked him with a hatchet.
General Adams had Alfred’s confession written down and made him sign it as a sworn statement.
Preston became so angry that he dragged Alfred outside and might have killed him if others had not intervened.
After the fight, Alfred was arrested for manslaughter and imprisoned in a log cabin owned by the sheriff of Saguache.
In the summer, General Adams took Alfred and some men into the mountains to try to recover the bodies, but they found nothing.
In August, while Alfred awaited trial, illustrator John Randolph traveled over the mountains.
As Randolph came down a pass to Lake City, he walked by a tributary of the Gunnison River near the spot where Alfred had said he left Shannon.
Randolph noticed something sticking out of the ground and then smelled a terrible stench.
Randolph found five men in different stages of decomposition.
One of the bodies was little more than bones, suggesting animals had gotten to it afterward.
Two of the men had been hit in the head with something blunt.
Another body was identified as Shannon Bell and had been stripped to the bones except for the hands and feet.
Shannon also appeared to have suffered a blunt-force injury to the head.
The remains showed deliberate removal of the edible portions, and except for the first man it did not look like animals had done it.
Randolph sketched the scene and then reported it to the authorities in Lake City.
A team of 20 volunteers later retrieved the bodies.
The coroner concluded that the men had been killed by blows to the head while they were asleep.
None of the bodies had defensive wounds or injuries, and they all had similar marks on their skulls.
The men had rags under their feet, suggesting they may have eaten the leather from their shoes after running out of food.
Investigators also found a track to a makeshift shelter.
The findings led investigators to speculate that Alfred had killed the men for their possessions, then become trapped by the weather and eaten them to survive.
Alfred’s charges were expected to be upgraded from manslaughter to first-degree murder.
Before the charges could be upgraded, someone gave Alfred a key, a penknife, and some food so he could escape.
The text says it is not clear who helped Alfred escape.
Alfred slipped out of his cell and was not seen again for nine years.
In 1883, one of the original prospectors who had stayed the winter with Chief Ouray opened a supply shop in Cheyenne, Wyoming.
On March 11, a man who called himself John Schwartze asked that shopkeeper to help him stock up for a planned trip.
The shopkeeper briefly thought the man was the John Schwartze he had known years earlier at a Native American camp, but he realized the man was Alfred Packer.
The shopkeeper told the local sheriff he had spotted a criminal.
Alfred was arrested and taken to Denver.
General Adams traveled to Denver to confirm that the prisoner was Alfred and then took him away for trial.
Adams asked Alfred again what had really happened all those years earlier.
Alfred then gave what would be his final story and what he largely stuck to until he died.
In Alfred’s final story, the party left Ouray’s camp with nowhere near enough food.
Alfred said the food was only enough for a single grown man for a week.
Alfred said a brutal snowstorm hit the party after two or three days.
Alfred said the men kept trekking until they reached the base of a mountain and then faced a deep valley with snow so deep they could barely walk.
Alfred said the party had to move to higher ground.
Alfred said that by day four they had only about a pint of flour left.
Alfred said that for about the next ten days the men lived only on rosebuds and pine gum while following a ridge above deeper snow.
Alfred said several of the men were in rough shape and cried out every night while praying to God for escape.
Alfred said the party eventually crossed the main ridge and went down into camp by a river.
Alfred said they followed the stream for a day until they reached a frozen lake, possibly Lake San Cristobal.
Alfred said the men decided to cross the lake to reach some trees for shelter.
Alfred said tensions were rising because the men were exhausted.
Alfred said Shannon acted stranger than usual one morning and may have been either planning to survive, going insane, or both.
Alfred said Shannon told him to explore higher on the mountain to find a way across.
Alfred said he took a pistol and set off but only found steep slopes and more snow.
Alfred said he admitted to General Adams for the first time that he was only partly a guide and did not really know what he was doing.
Alfred said he spent all day scouting ahead and returning.
Alfred said that when he got back he found Shannon sitting by the fire eating a piece of meat.
Alfred said he saw a dead man lying a short distance from the fire.
Alfred said he then saw the other three men lying around the fire and not moving.
Alfred said he shot Shannon in the stomach before Shannon could reach him and then finished him after he fell.
In a later letter, Alfred wrote of “the midnight horrors of starvation as well as those of utter isolation.”
Alfred said he felt himself losing his sanity and understood what happened to Shannon because it was beginning to happen to him.
In another letter, Alfred said, “The greatest wonder is that I ever returned to a rational condition.”
The next morning, Alfred tried to follow his tracks from the previous day but had to turn back because of the snow and his exhaustion.
Alfred then built a small shelter from wood and branches.
Alfred said the shelter did not satisfy his growing hunger.
Alfred concluded that hunting was not a reliable source of food.
In desperation, Alfred took the piece of meat Shannon had been eating, cooked it, and ate it.
Alfred said the relief of eating overcame the horror of cannibalism.
Alfred said he spent another two months in the shelter surviving off the rest of his party.
Sixty days later, Alfred saw an avalanche that left yellow clay behind.
Alfred took this as evidence that he was in Slumgullion Pass, which was named for its yellow color and for its resemblance to Slumgullion stew.
In early spring, Alfred finally knew where he was and set off up the mountain again.
Before leaving, Alfred gathered some of the remaining meat and wrapped it to eat while walking.
Alfred also checked the other men’s pockets and found the money he later spent in Saguache.
Alfred had already eaten his shoes, so he wrapped his feet in cloth.
Sometimes Alfred had to stop because his feet began to freeze.
When his feet froze, Alfred lit a fire to warm them.
When he neared the agency, Alfred ate the last pieces of meat and may have dropped some that the Ute later found.
Alfred said he wanted to take them farther to show them the truth, but he also did not want to return and be reminded of the horror.
Alfred said he escaped and ran from trial because he feared a mob might get past his guard and kill him.
Alfred said he had already nearly been killed by Preston Nutter and thought someone else would eventually finish the job.
After escaping, Alfred said he went to Arkansas under a fake name and worked on a ranch.
Alfred said he later moved to Arizona and then traveled to Cheyenne, where he was found.
Alfred’s trial called into question several parts of his story.
The prosecution argued that Alfred had deliberately and premeditatedly led the men astray in order to steal their possessions by any means necessary.
The prosecution said Alfred’s survival story was an attempt to cover up his crimes.
The prosecution called numerous witnesses to support this theory.
Some witnesses came from the original Utah party.
Preston testified that Alfred constantly tried to find out how much money the others had.
Other witnesses testified about Alfred’s behavior after he reached Saguache and the changing stories he told.
When Alfred testified, he spoke for six hours and admitted eating the other men, but he insisted that only he killed Shannon and that Shannon was responsible for everything else.
After all the evidence was heard, the jury found Alfred guilty of premeditated murder, theft, and several other charges.
Alfred was sentenced to be hanged.
Alfred’s lawyers found a technicality before the hanging could occur.
Colorado became a state in 1876, and before statehood Colorado Territory had no statute under which Alfred could be tried for murder.
The murder laws Alfred was tried under were not established until after the crime had occurred.
Because of that, Alfred’s murder conviction was overturned.
In the new trial, Alfred again pleaded not guilty and repeated his story.
The new case was even more damaging to Alfred.
Hunters testified that there was plenty of food available even in a bad winter.
The hunters said game, rabbits, deer, and other food would have been easy to hunt even for someone as inexperienced as Alfred.
The hunters also claimed that the cannibalism must have been by choice because food would have been available.
Other witnesses were brought in to testify about Alfred's behavior after he reached Saguache and the different accounts he gave of the events.
When Alfred finally took the stand, his testimony did not help his case.
Alfred was sentenced to be hanged for his crimes.
Before statehood, Colorado Territory did not have a murder statute under which Alfred could be tried.
Colorado State established the specific laws for the crime only after the crime had already taken place.
The prosecution argued that the cannibalism had to have been by choice because food was plentiful in the area.
The prosecution also argued that Alfred at the very least led the group astray by hiking a more dangerous route in winter under the guise of being a guide.
The prosecution said that in the best case Alfred was extremely negligent.
Alfred was eventually found guilty of voluntary manslaughter.
For the voluntary manslaughter conviction, he received 40 years in prison.
The 40-year term was the maximum of 8 years per man.
At the time, the sentence was the longest prison sentence handed down in US history.
After being imprisoned, Alfred wrote to anyone he could and claimed the sentence was unjust.
Alfred said he had only killed Shannon and that the jury was full of biased and prejudiced people.
Alfred's story eventually reached a woman named Polly Pry.
Polly Pry was a reporter for the Denver Post.
After hearing Alfred's story, Polly Pry believed him somewhat.
She wrote stories about him that made him out to be a man of the people.
She described him as an ex-soldier persecuted by the establishment and as someone who survived horrors most people could not imagine.
She said his sentence was so harsh because of the cannibalism, but that anyone would have done the same in that situation.
Polly Pry's stories became influential enough that local businesses started arranging petitions for Alfred's release.
After enough pressure, the Colorado governor paroled Alfred in 1901.
Alfred was paroled 18 years into his sentence.
In the century after the story, several different groups performed separate forensic analyses of the remains and compared them to Alfred's account.
Those groups tended to conclude that Alfred was guilty.
Some of the analyses found defensive wounds on bones from the group, which contradicted Alfred's account.
One group found marks across Shannon Bell's forearms that indicated he may have defended himself from an attack.
In Alfred's account, Shannon was only shot once and then finished quickly.
In 1994, an 1862 Colt revolver was found at the site of the murders.
The revolver was still loaded with three .38-caliber bullets.
Those bullets matched some fragments of lead found in Shandon Bell's hip.
The bullet match suggested that at least part of Alfred's story may have been true.
After prison, Alfred seemed to be a changed man.
He worked at the Denver Post as a guard for a while.
People described Alfred as kind, modest, and even charitable after prison.
Those descriptions contrasted with the grumpy, greedy, and untrustworthy man he had been in the past.
Alfred eventually moved to Littleton.
In Littleton, Alfred bought a copper mine and went back into prospecting.
Alfred died in 1907 at age 65.
Rumor had it that Alfred was a vegetarian when he died.
SRC_2: Alferd E. Packer lived from 1842 to 1909 and was also called “Alfred.”
Packer was a prospector who became famous after confessing to eating his dead comrades while trapped in the San Juan Mountains in February 1874.
The text says it appears likely that Packer killed another prospector in self-defense before he began gnawing on the corpses of those who had already died.
Packer’s cannibalism story is presented as highlighting the dangers faced by nearly every nineteenth-century prospector who ventured into the Rocky Mountains.
Packer’s story has become one of the West’s most grisly and enduring legends and murder mysteries.
Packer had been part of a larger band of twenty gold seekers who left Utah and split into two groups.
On February 9, 1874, Al Packer and five other prospectors departed the Ute leader Ouray’s winter camp.
The prospectors ignored Ouray’s warning and declined his offer to let them stay before heading into deep snow.
Packer later said that three or four days after their provisions were gone, the men cooked their raw-hide moccasins.
Packer later said that when their trail was drifted over, they gathered wild rose buds, stewed them, and ate them.
Packer left Utah with few provisions and no weapons.
Nine weeks later Packer arrived at the Los Piños Indian Agency south of present-day Gunnison with a Winchester rifle, a skinning knife, and a coffee pot containing live coals.
When he reached the Los Piños Indian Agency, Packer was haggard and worn but otherwise fit.
Packer played high-stakes poker at Dolan’s saloon and bought a $70 horse.
Another member of the original gold seekers questioned where Packer had gotten his spending money.
Packer admitted that the small band had starved in the San Juans, that Israel Swan had died from hunger and exposure, and that Packer had eaten him.
Packer was jailed in Saguache, escaped, changed his identity, and was arrested in Wyoming before being returned to Hinsdale County for trial.
The area northeast of Lake City where Packer’s party got lost is labeled “Cannibal Plateau” on maps.
The site where the bodies were found five miles beyond town is called Deadman’s Gulch.
After being re-captured, Packer said Shannon Bell killed James Humphrey, George Noon, and Frank Miller as they slept around the campfire while the group tried to find the Indian Agency.
Packer said that when he returned from searching for food, Shannon Bell accosted him with a hatchet.
Packer said he fired twice with a pistol and shot Bell in self-defense.
Packer said that after killing Bell he lived on the flesh of the dead men for the greater part of the sixty days he was out.
Packer’s lawyer mounted a spirited defense, but Packer went to prison for seventeen years before The Denver Post petitioned for his release.
In prison, Packer made horsehair bridles, and one is displayed at the Museum of Western Colorado in Grand Junction.
In prison, Packer also built elaborate Victorian dollhouses.
Packer died in 1907, and the text says his misspelled name and unique reputation live on.
The text says Packer evolved from Old West infamy to New West celebrity.
In the 1950s, a rusted 1862 Colt Police Model .32 five-shot revolver was found on the Cannibal Plateau with two shots missing.
Analysis at Mesa State College’s Electron Microscopy Facility matched bullet fragments from the burial site to lead from the old pistol.
The bullet match suggested that Packer did shoot Shannon Bell in self-defense.
Museum curator David Bailey said Packer did not deny eating the bodies, killed only in self-defense, and was wrongly convicted.
Packer’s pistol is now on display at the Museum of Western Colorado.
In Lake City, “Al Packer Days,” the Packer Burger at the Cannibal Grill, and a large wooden marker for the Alferd Packer Massacre Site are popular attractions.
Travel magazines say the Hinsdale County Museum has “the largest collection of Packer memorabilia known.”
The magazines say the collection includes skull fragments, clothing buttons from victims, and the shackles used when Packer was imprisoned.
Tourists are advised not to miss the actual burial site, which is just five minutes from town.
In 1968, students at the University of Colorado in Boulder renamed the student union restaurant the Alferd E. Packer Memorial Grill.
In 1998, author James E. Bank wrote Alferd Packer’s Wilderness Cookbook.
CU film students Matt Stone and Trey Parker produced Cannibal! The Musical in 1993.
Matt Stone and Trey Parker later created the TV show South Park.
The text says Cannibal! The Musical was short-lived, like Packer’s companions.
SRC_3: Alfred Griner Packer was born on January 21, 1842, in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, near Pittsburgh.
Alfred Griner Packer died on April 23, 1907, in Jefferson County, Colorado, at age 65.
Packer was also known as John Schwartze and the Colorado Cannibal.
Packer was known for cannibalism.
Packer’s convictions were murder, which was later overturned, and five counts of voluntary manslaughter.
Packer’s criminal penalty was death, which was commuted to 40 years in prison.
Packer was an American prospector and self-proclaimed wilderness guide.
Packer confessed to cannibalism during the winter of 1874.
The text says no clear or definitive evidence has yet been found to prove Packer’s deeds.
The text says he is one of four people historically convicted for cannibalism in the United States.
Packer emerged as the sole survivor of a six-man party that tried to travel through the San Juan Mountains of the Colorado Territory.
Packer gave more than one version of his account of the circumstances surrounding the deaths of his companions.
After his story was questioned, Packer escaped jail and hid from justice for nine years.
He was eventually tried, convicted of premeditated murder, and sentenced to death.
Packer won a retrial and was eventually sentenced to 40 years in prison on five counts of voluntary manslaughter.
The Legend of Alfred Packer, an almost completely fictitious biopic of his exploits, was released in 1980.
Cannibal! The Musical, a more comedic and heavily fabricated version of the story, was released in 1993.
Packer’s father moved the family to LaGrange County, Indiana, by the early 1850s and worked there as a cabinetmaker.
Packer moved to Minnesota in his late teens and worked as a shoemaker.
Packer enlisted in the Union army on April 22, 1862, in Winona, Minnesota, and was assigned to Company F of the 16th Infantry Regiment.
Packer was honorably discharged eight months later because of epilepsy, which had triggered seizures.
Packer enlisted in the 8th Iowa Cavalry Regiment at Ottumwa, Iowa, on June 25, 1863.
Packer received a second discharge on April 22, 1864, because of epilepsy.
Packer worked as a hunter, wagon teamster, ranch hand, field worker, guide, miner, and other mining-related laborer as he traveled west over the next nine years.
People who knew Packer during this period later said he was ill-suited to being a guide and prone to losing his way.
Most people who knew Packer disliked and distrusted him because of his argumentative personality, his nearly pathological lying, and his reputation for theft.
Robert McGrue assembled a party of 20 in Salt Lake City to travel to the San Juan Mountains after hearing of gold discovered in Breckenridge.
The party left in November 1873.
George Tracy said the party met a 23-year-old Alfred Packer near Provo.
Packer said he wanted to join the party, claimed he was a prospector and guide who knew the San Juan territory well, and offered $25 to join because he had no provisions.
The prospectors accepted Packer’s help because they needed a guide.
Members of McGrue’s party later said Packer had overstated or possibly fabricated his experience with the area.
Packer was reported to have had only a Colt revolver and no rifle when the expedition left.
Party members reported that Packer was greedy with rations, lazy, obstinate, and obsessed with how much money the others had brought.
Packer quarreled constantly with Frank Miller.
Preston Nutter later called Packer a “whining fraud” at the time of the first trial.
Packer’s epileptic seizures made his presence in the group strenuous.
Rumors said Packer had spent time in jail in Salt Lake City on a charge of murdering a hunting partner.
The party moved more slowly than expected toward Breckenridge despite Packer’s presence as a guide.
Winter crippled the wagons and horses.
While traveling the Spanish Trail, the party encountered heavy snow that hid the path and forced them to rely almost entirely on a compass.
The party became lost because of Packer’s inexperience.
Provisions ran out, and the men survived first on horse feed and were nearly at the point of eating the horses.
On January 21, 1874, the party came to Chief Ouray’s camp near Montrose, Colorado, in the Uncompahgre Valley.
Chief Ouray supplied the party with food and lodging and urged them to wait until spring because the mountains were dangerous in winter.
Ouray said no Ute would attempt such a journey and that doing so would risk almost certain death.
Ouray offered to let the men stay with his tribe until winter ended and promised to share what he and his people had.
Despite Ouray’s warnings, 11 men decided to continue on.
The men planned to travel first to the Los Pinós Indian Agency, the closest outpost to the camp, and then continue to Breckenridge.
Ouray gave the men food for the journey and safe directions to avoid the mountains.
Packer wanted to reach the agency by going through the mountains because he said it was a more direct route.
The party split into two groups, with five men following Oliver Loutsenhizer along the Gunnison River and six, including Packer, heading through the San Juan Mountains.
Loutsenhizer threatened to shoot Packer if he tried to follow the other group.
On February 9, Packer and five others left for the Los Pinós Indian Agency, which was 75 miles ahead.
The lack of opposition in the other group to Packer’s departure led many researchers to conclude that his inexperience and attitude had become taxing and that they were better off without him.
Bob McGrue guided Packer’s group along the river route advised by Chief Ouray until his horses could not continue.
McGrue unloaded the men’s provisions and returned to Ouray’s camp.
Packer then led his group higher into the San Juan Mountains, disregarding Ouray’s warning.

The men entered the mountains with food barely sufficient for the supposed 14-day journey on the safest route, no snowshoes, only a bare minimum of matches, no flint, no heavy clothing, two rifles, one pistol, a couple of knives, a hatchet, and minimal ammunition.
On April 16, 1874, 65 days after his departure, Packer emerged alone from the woods and crossed a frozen lake bed to the Los Pinós Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado.
Packer arrived at the agency while the men there were eating breakfast and begged for food and shelter.
He carried a rifle, a knife, a steel coffee pot, and a satchel.
Packer vomited when given food and said his digestion had been altered by prolonged near-starvation.
Packer told the agency men that he had been hired by five men to guide them to Breckenridge.
Packer said he became snow-blind, fell behind the party, and became a burden.
Packer claimed that Israel Swan gave him a rifle before the others abandoned him.
Packer said he survived alone on roots and rose buds and had also eaten his moccasins.
The agency men found it odd that Packer did not look as malnourished and threadbare as other lost wanderers after more than two months in the wilderness.
Packer’s face was reported as bloated and his body was hardly skeletal.
Packer said he would drink whisky for breakfast instead of food.
Packer said he was broke and sold the Winchester rifle he carried to Major Downer for $10.
Packer stayed at the agency for ten days before going to Saguache to buy supplies for his trip back home to Pennsylvania.
In Saguache, Packer bought a horse for $70 and booked a room at Dolan’s Saloon.
Larry Dolan later said Packer spent around $100 during his stay and offered to lend him $300.
Packer spent an additional $78 in Otto Mears’ general store.
It was also claimed that Packer had several different wallets in his possession.
Preston Nutter later arrived in Saguache with two other original party members and found Packer in Dolan’s Saloon.
When Nutter asked about the rest of the party, Packer said he had “got his feet wet and frozen.”
Packer said a winter storm hit after the men set up camp, that he started a fire while the others went ahead for food, and that Swan left him his rifle and never returned.
Nutter thought Packer’s story was odd because five miners unfamiliar with Colorado would not likely abandon their guide in snowbound mountains.
Nutter also found it strange that Swan would give Packer his rifle, leaving four men with only one rifle.
When Nutter asked about the knife, Packer said Miller had stuck it in a tree and walked off without it.
Nutter fought with Packer and later described him as sulky, obstinate, quarrelsome, and a petty thief.
Two men from the five-man Gunnison River group eventually arrived at the Los Pinós Indian Agency, and the remaining three arrived a few days later.
The men were introduced to General Charles Adams, who said he had already met Alfred Packer and heard from him that his companions had deserted him.
All five men immediately discredited Packer’s account and said the men they knew would never abandon a man to die.
Loutsenhizer told Adams that Packer was not to be trusted and that he suspected Packer’s stories.
Loutsenhizer said the Winchester rifle Packer carried belonged to an elderly man in the party and that a pipe Packer left at the agency belonged to Shannon Bell.
The men persuaded Adams to send a mounted officer to Saguache to retrieve Packer for questioning while pretending to recruit him for a search party.
Packer was preparing to leave Saguache when Nutter and other men approached him again.
Packer reluctantly agreed and rode back to Los Pinós with the officer.
After arriving at the agency again, Packer met General Adams and five men he had not seen since February.

The agency officer told Adams that Nutter said Packer had spent several hundred dollars in Saguache, bought a new horse and saddle, possessed items belonging to missing men, and had originally joined the party penniless.
Loutsenhizer demanded an explanation, and Packer repeated the same story he had told before.
Packer said he was surprised the men had not been heard from and said he was concerned for their welfare.
When asked where his wealth came from, Packer said he had received a cash loan from a man in Saguache.
The officer returned saying multiple sources had seen Packer with several wallets, heard him tell varying stories, seen him arrive with cash, and knew of no one who had lent him money.
As Adams and others were settling the matter, two Ute men arrived in Los Piños with strips of dried human flesh they had found on a hill near the agency.
Packer begged for mercy and said, “It would not be the first time that people had been obliged to eat each other when they were hungry.”
Herman Lauter transcribed Packer’s first official statement.
In his first official statement, Packer said the men left Ouray’s camp with what they believed was enough food for a 14-day trip.
Packer said provisions ran out sooner than expected.
Packer said that after days of almost no wildlife activity and almost no food, the men began to eye one another in an unsettling way.
Packer said he left camp to gather dry firewood and returned to find four men around the body of Israel Swan, who had been struck in the head with a hatchet and killed instantly.
Packer said several thousand dollars was found on Swan and divided among the men.
Packer said they ate the most agreeable parts of Swan’s body, packed some of it, and continued on with Swan’s rifle.
Packer said the five men ran out of meat again within two days and that game continued to elude them.
Packer said Bell, Humphrey, Noon, and he secretly decided that Miller would be next.
Packer said Miller was chosen because he was stocky and had a lot of soft flesh.
Packer said Miller was killed by a hatchet blow to the head while stooping to pick up firewood.
Packer said Bell and he agreed not to eat each other and had a rifle each plus a couple thousand dollars of Swan’s cash.
Packer said they expected two men to survive the rest of the journey with the little game available.
Packer said they agreed to claim the four others died from exposure and were buried with dignity.
Packer said they vowed never to speak of the cannibalism because they thought no one would believe it was necessary.
After several days of travel and little food beyond a rabbit and some roots, Packer said Bell suddenly screamed that he could not take it anymore and that one of them would die for food.
Packer said Bell rushed at him with a rifle, intending to strike his skull, and that Packer deflected the blow and hit Bell in the head with a hatchet.
Packer said he butchered Bell, ate as much as he could, packed more away, took Bell’s share of Swan’s money, and continued toward the agency.
Packer said he threw away the remaining strips of Bell’s flesh after seeing the Los Pinós Indian Agency from a hill.
General Adams called a conference of the five men and the agency officers to decide what to do next.
The five original party members said they did not believe any part of Packer’s story.
The Ute men said there was a place next to a lake about 50 miles away across the hills that matched Packer’s description.
A search party led by Herman Lauter and consisting of the five Utah miners, several agency officers, and Packer as guide was sent out.
After two weeks, near the Lake Fork of the Gunnison River, Packer said he was lost and did not recognize the area.
The search party found nothing and returned to the agency.
On the way back, Packer tried to murder Herman Lauter with a knife.
Packer was caught, restrained, and arrested for the attack on Lauter.
General Adams, who had previously been willing to believe Packer, became convinced Packer was dangerous after the unprovoked attack on his officer.
Packer was taken to Saguache and jailed outside town by the sheriff for his own protection.
While detained, Packer retracted his earlier account of how the five men died.
In his new account, Packer said the men encountered a strong blizzard in the mountains.
Packer said the snow was so heavy and persistent that they became hopelessly lost and could not retrace their steps.
Packer said they ran out of matches and had to carry hot embers in a steel coffee pot to light fires.
Packer said the men found no game for days and that attempts at ice fishing failed completely.
Packer said they roasted and ate their shoes and tried to survive on scant edible vegetation.
Packer said the men made a pact that if one died, his meat would save the others from starvation.
Packer said that after days of hiking with almost nothing to eat, Israel Swan could go no further and died from hunger and exposure.
In Packer’s signed first confession, he said Old Man Swan died first and was eaten by the other five people about ten days out of camp.
In the signed confession, Packer said Humphreys died four or five days later and was also eaten, and that Humphreys had about $133.
In the signed confession, Packer said he found Humphreys’ pocketbook and took the money.
In the signed confession, Packer said the butcher was later killed accidentally by the other two and was also eaten.
In the signed confession, Packer said Bell shot “California” with Swan’s gun and that Packer killed Bell by shooting him.
In the signed confession, Packer said he covered the remains and took a large piece with him before traveling 14 days into the agency.
In the signed confession, Packer said Bell wanted to kill him with his rifle and struck a tree instead, breaking the gun.
In Packer’s later amended version, the men had endured almost 20 days from Ouray’s camp and more than 10 days without any substantial food.
In the amended version, Packer said James Humphrey died of exposure to extreme cold.
In the amended version, Packer said Bell later rushed at him with a rifle, intending to bludgeon him, and that Packer shot Bell with his pistol.
Packer confessed to taking the valuables of the deceased members because they no longer needed them.
While Packer was in jail, observers challenged his credibility and noted that he was not, as the truncated text says, a victim of cold.
Packer said he found a pocketbook, took $133 from it, and later was carrying wood when the butcher was killed and eaten.
While Packer was in jail, observers said he was probably not a victim of cold or starvation and had instead led his group into the hills to kill and rob them.
In the following August, John A. Randolph found the site of the incident.
Randolph was an illustrator who worked for Harper's Weekly magazine.
Randolph discovered all five bodies at the foot of Slumgullion Pass, two miles southeast of Lake City, Colorado, in a pine-shaded gulch.
The bodies lay above the Lake Fork of the Gunnison River, now called Dead Man's Gulch.
The location matched Packer's original claim that only Bell was killed there.
The snow covering the bodies and campsite had melted in the intervening four months.
Randolph sketched the scene and alerted authorities in nearby Lake City.
Harper's Weekly covered the story on October 17, 1874, and included Randolph's illustration.
The local coroner and law enforcement went to the site with about 20 volunteers.
They found the bodies of all five men in different states of decomposition after four months left to the elements and animals.
First responders said it appeared that extreme violence had befallen the men.
Frank Miller's head was missing from the campsite.
Frank Miller's and Israel Swan's corpses had been heavily worked over by scavengers and were little more than scattered bones.
Israel Swan's skull had a jagged chunk missing.
George Noon and James Humphrey were mostly flayed torsos of rotting viscera attached to skeletal legs.
Noon and Humphrey still had intact bearded faces, with Humphrey's face more decayed than Noon's.
Noon and Humphrey had head blows whose shape suggested a hatchet, and their bodies had noticeable broken bones.
Shannon Bell had skeletal legs, arms cut crudely to the bones, and hands that were still fully skinned.
Bell's remaining corpse was a mass of viscera inside an almost wholly flayed torso.
Bell still had a thick red beard and bushy hair on his face.
Bell's face showed little decay, suggesting he was the last to die.
The top of Bell's skull had been ripped open.
The three bodies that were still intact or partly intact had flesh and muscle cut from choice and meaty locations.
No attempt had been made to consume bone marrow or any organs.
The state of the bodies contradicted Packer's version of events.
The bodies were all together in one spot rather than scattered across miles.
Humphrey and Noon still had large portions of flesh, muscle, and organs that could have been eaten before Bell allegedly tried to murder Packer.
The men had tattered cloths lashed to their rotting feet, replacing shoes they probably ate.
Moldy and tattered blankets lay beneath and beside the bodies.
A beaten path ran from the corpses to a crude shelter used by Packer.
Evidence suggested the deaths happened before supplies were totally exhausted.
Within the shelter were possessions of the men that Packer had left behind.
Preston Nutter accompanied the party to the site and identified the bodies as the five missing men.
A rifle broken in two was found near the bodies.
Because of the damage on the remains, the broken rifle was presumed to have been used to bludgeon one or more of the men.
Officials buried the remains at the site.
Packer's jail was little more than a log cabin on ranch property belonging to the Saguache County Sheriff.
Months passed with no definitive evidence of a crime, no bodies discovered, and no formal charges lodged against Packer other than the attempt on Lauter's life.
Saguache County authorities were reportedly unhappy about taxpayer money being spent to keep Packer housed and guarded.
Packer was allegedly given a makeshift key for his irons and some supplies, and he escaped easily.
Nearly all of Saguache believed Packer was guilty of robbery or murder.
Packer's life was constantly threatened by nearby townspeople.
Packer never said who helped him escape, how it happened, or why.
It was presumed that either Packer bribed his guard or someone else did.
The generally accepted theory at the time was that Packer falsely claimed to be a mountain guide familiar with the area in order to accompany the men to Breckenridge.
That theory held that he led his party to miserable deaths through gross incompetence.
A more popular theory was that Packer left Ouray's camp with five men and planned to lead them into the wilderness to kill and rob them.
Nutter and Loutsenhizer tried to discredit Packer's claimed qualifications as a guide and pointed to his character flaws, inconsistent stories, and contradictions.
Local papers gave the story constant coverage with sensational headlines and negative comments about Packer.
The incident drew national and international attention.
Nearly the entire population of Saguache and soon nearly the entire country believed Packer was culpable for the deaths.
Cannibalism was not seen as the main issue in his guilt.
People at the time knew the Donner Party story and understood that people sometimes ate the dead in wilderness emergencies.
Cannibalism is not illegal per se in the United States unless a person commits murder to obtain the flesh.
In such a case, the accused would be charged with murder, and the cannibalism would be charged as desecration or abuse of a corpse.
Packer later claimed he had been unjustly vilified and convicted for cannibalism rather than for murder.
On March 11, 1883, Jean "Frenchy" Cabazon found Packer in Cheyenne, Wyoming, living under the alias "John Schwartze".
John Schwartze was one of the original members of the Utah mining party who stayed in Chief Ouray's camp in the winter of 1874.
Cabazon was a member of the original party that left Provo and had stayed in Chief Ouray's camp before reaching their destination with Bob McGrue and Preston Nutter's party.
Packer approached Cabazon looking to buy supplies.
Cabazon reported Packer to the local sheriff, who apprehended him and contacted General Adams.
Cabazon was summoned to Cheyenne, confirmed Packer's identity, and accompanied him by train to Denver for Packer's second confession.
Packer signed the second confession on March 16.
Packer said his main reason for fleeing was fear of mob justice from the populace of Saguache.
Because the actual crime occurred within Hinsdale County rather than neighboring Saguache County, Packer was sent to Lake City for detention and prosecution.
In the second confession, Packer said Bell had killed the others after telling him to scout for a way out of the mountains and for food.
Packer said he returned in the late evening after being gone most of the day.
Packer told General Adams that Bell was roasting meat cut from Miller's leg and that Miller's body lay farthest from the fire down the stream with his skull crushed by a hatchet.
Packer told Adams that the other three bodies were near the fire with hatchet cuts in the forehead.

Packer said he came within a rod of the fire, Bell came toward him with a hatchet, Packer shot Bell sideways through the belly, Bell fell on his face, and Packer struck him in the top of the head with the hatchet.
Packer said he dropped his revolver in deep snow and lost it.
Packer said he made a crude shelter from stray logs to fight the snow and wind away from the bodies.
Packer said another storm set in and he hunkered down for hours.
Packer said he was starving and had to eat something or die.

Packer said he returned to the fire, covered the men, took the piece of meat near the fire back to camp, made a new fire, cooked and ate it, and then lived off the flesh of the men for the bigger part of sixty days.
When Adams asked why he had not told this story nine years earlier, Packer said he was excited and the story came first to his mind.
At the time of Packer's trial, Israel Swan's family reported that he had gone on the expedition with about $6,000 in cash and gold.
Israel Swan's family also reported that Swan carried a valuable Winchester rifle.
Swan's age of 65 was said to give Packer a strong motive for murder.
The other four members may have been complicit in Swan's murder and later betrayed by Packer, or murdered by Packer for being witnesses.
Packer was not found with any gold at arrest, and the money he still had did not total in the thousands.
Packer's spending had been frivolous.
On April 6, a trial began in Lake City.
The prosecution argued that the only logical reason for Packer to attempt such a perilous journey with minimal food and supplies was to lead the men into the wilderness to kill and rob them.
Packer pleaded not guilty.
After seven days of testimony and examination, he was found guilty of the premeditated murder of Israel Swan.
Packer was sentenced to death by hanging scheduled for May 19, 1883.
It was presumed that Swan died on or around March 1.
The prosecution said Swan's remains showed signs of a struggle at death and that the others appeared to have been killed in their sleep.
Otto Mears, Larry Dolan, Oliver D. Loutsenhizer, and Preston Nutter testified for the prosecution, and Nutter was the key witness.
A local newspaper quoted Judge M.B. Gerry as saying a highly insulting sentence in dialect.
Court records show Judge Gerry's sentence in conventional apolitical language.
Packer's lawyers found that the 1874 murder statutes had been repealed and replaced with a savings clause.
In October 1885, the Colorado Supreme Court reversed the sentence on ex post facto grounds.
The court said the government could not sentence a man to death for a crime committed before Colorado became a state if the crime had occurred at all.
The overturned murder charge and execution did not end Packer's culpability for the deaths.
A second trial was held in Gunnison after a change of venue granted by the Colorado Supreme Court.
The second trial also had a new Republican judge presiding.
Packer and his counsel believed the prejudices and presumed guilt in Lake City, where most people were Democrats, made a fair trial impossible.
Packer again pleaded not guilty.
The sentence was eight years for each count, the maximum allowed per count.
At the time, the 40-year term was the longest custodial sentence in U.S. history.
Local hunters and officials said the winter of 1874 was very bad but that the San Juan camp area still had plenty of deer, antelope, and smaller game.
There was also a report that a deer carcass was found near the campsite.
This damaged Packer's claim that the area was so lacking in wildlife that cannibalism was quickly necessary.
The route Packer chose through the San Juan Mountains in midwinter was described as practically suicidal.
Locals had given him a safe route beside a main water source that could have provided fresh fish and kept them on course.
Packer instead chose a mountain path with minimal supplies because he wrongly believed it would be faster.
In fact, the route Packer and his companions took was nearly the same length as the recommended route but much more dangerous.
Packer testified in his own defense at the second hearing.
His account of the campsite events remained largely the same as his second official version.
Packer asked to be charged 40 years only for the death of Shannon Bell, whom he said he alone had killed.
The request was denied.
Packer was sent to the Canon City Penitentiary to serve his sentence.
Packer filed appeals five times and was denied each time.
He sent letters to local newspapers saying he had been unjustly convicted by an unfair and unsympathetic judicial system and by ignorant small-minded people.
On June 19, 1899, the Colorado Supreme Court officially upheld his sentence.
Packer was paroled on February 8, 1901.
His parole followed a campaign led by Duane Hatch, who petitioned for his release for nearly a decade before Polly Pry learned of it.
Packer had served 18 years of his 40-year sentence.

Polly Pry of The Denver Post used Packer's Army service to portray him as a common man and a victim of circumstances who had been crucified for violating civilized sensibilities by resorting to cannibalism.
Pry's stories helped change the minds of local businesses and people, leading to petitions sent to Colorado Governor Charles Thomas.
Thomas ultimately relented and, as his last official act before leaving office, paroled but did not pardon Packer on the condition that he would not try to profit from his story.
After parole, Packer worked as a guard at The Denver Post and later as a ranch hand.
Many believed his job at The Denver Post resulted directly from Pry and her employers securing his release.
Packer respected Pry for the rest of his life and called her his Liberator.
His cause of death was cited as "Dementia – trouble & worry".
His clinical cause of death has been described as a stroke.
Packer was widely rumored to have become a vegetarian before his death.
People who knew him said he was rich with stories, liked by children, lived modestly, and was charitable.
Packer was buried in Littleton, Colorado.
His grave has a veteran's tombstone listing his original regiment in 1862 because his original grave marker was stolen.
His first name is listed as Alfred, and he was known to use both "Alfred" and "Alferd" in life.
He was never successful in getting an official state pardon.
The Littleton Cemetery Association cemented over Packer's grave in 1973 to deter grave robbing and vandalism.
Edward Meyer of Ripley's Believe It or Not! Museum said the museum had Packer's dissected skull bought from an anonymous party for $20,000.
No statement was made about how the skull's authenticity was verified, other than that the seller's origin information was sufficient.
If the skull is Packer's, it is presumed that his head was removed shortly before or after burial, dissected, had the brain removed for study, and was preserved by arsenic curing.
The skull is said to have later gone to a traveling sideshow, then to a private party, and then to Ripley's.
As of 2008, the skull was reported to be at the Ripley's Museum in San Antonio, Texas, after relocation from New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina.
On July 17, 1989, James E. Starrs led an exhumation of the five bodies 115 years after Packer consumed his companions.
Starrs was a law professor specializing in forensic science at George Washington University.
The remains were found at the end of a residential driveway belonging to a local surgeon and buried only 13 inches below ground level.
Starrs and Walter H. Birkby said they did not think cannibalism could ever be scientifically demonstrated unless a person actually saw the eating.
Because Packer never denied cannibalism, that was not the main purpose of the investigation.
The evidence led Starrs to conclude that Packer had murdered his comrades.
Starrs believed Packer more likely murdered his companions for their belongings and resorted to cannibalism out of necessity rather than intent.
The men were reinterred and given a proper burial with funeral rites.
Exhumation of the remains showed blunt force trauma to the skulls of two men and no other notable disturbance except butchering marks.
All skulls had damage of varying extent to their upper craniums.
Fabric fibers were found in some skulls, suggesting their heads may have been covered with a blanket at the time of death.
The three other skeletons showed defensive hacking marks across the radial and ulna bones of their forearms, including Shannon Bell's.
Those marks could have been sustained while shielding the face and body from an attack.
No other noteworthy disturbance was found in the skeletal remains except damage made during butchering.
Packer claimed that Bell had murdered the others with hatchet blows to the head, but in his second version of the story he never claimed he had to fight Bell with the hatchet in any rendition.
In one version of Packer’s story, Bell charged at him with Swan’s rifle and Packer shot him.
In Packer’s second official version, he said he finished off Bell with a hatchet blow to the head, and that was the extent of his hatchet claim.
All five skeletons had numerous differing post-mortem injuries, including depressed fractures, butterfly fractures, butchering trauma, and hacking trauma.
These injuries seem to contradict Packer’s claim of “minimal cannibalism.”
Two skeletons other than Shannon Bell’s were found to have cylindrical puncture wounds in the pelvic bone.
Some people have questioned whether the three pelvic marks were scavenging marks from a bear or possibly bullet wounds.
No definitive conclusions have been made about the cylindrical puncture wounds.
The discovery suggested a scenario in which two men were bludgeoned in their sleep by Packer.
In that scenario, the three remaining men awoke and Packer shot them in the hips to incapacitate them if the punctures were bullet wounds.
In that scenario, the three men then tried to fight off Packer while he wielded a hatchet, and he killed them all with blows to the head.
In that scenario, Packer butchered the men and used their flesh to survive in snowbound conditions during his journey.
The differing states of decomposition contradict that theory, although it remains plausible.
It seems unlikely that Packer shot three of the five men in the hip unless he intended to debilitate them before killing them.
No entry and exit geometry analysis has been done to date that could clarify the initial cause of the injuries.
Packer’s ultimate motivation for the murders has been heavily debated and has several possible theories.
In 1994, David P. Bailey, Curator of History at the Museum of Western Colorado, began an investigation to seek more conclusive results than Starrs about Packer’s claim of having shot Bell.
Among the Audrey Thrailkill collection of firearms at the museum was a Colt revolver that reportedly had been found at the site of Packer’s alleged crime.
Exhaustive investigation into the pistol’s background turned up trial-era documents.
A Civil War veteran who visited the crime scene said Shannon Bell had been shot twice and the other victims had been killed with a hatchet.
The same veteran said he noticed a severe bullet wound to Bell’s pelvic area and a bullet hole through Bell’s wallet.
These documents seem to corroborate Packer’s claim that Bell killed the other victims and that Packer shot Bell in self-defense.
By 2000, Bailey had not yet proven a link between the antique pistol and Alfred Packer.
Bailey discovered that forensic samples from the 1989 exhumation had been archived.
In 2001, Dr. Richard Dujay at Mesa State College analyzed the archived samples with an electron microscope.
Dujay found microscopic lead fragments in the soil taken from under Shannon Bell’s remains.
The lead fragments were matched by spectrograph with bullets remaining in Packer’s pistol.
At least Bell appears to have been shot, but whether the shooting was self-defense remains unanswered.
In Dashiell Hammett’s novel The Thin Man, Nick Charles advises Gilbert Wynant to read a selection about Packer’s expeditions.
The selection comes from Thomas Samuel Duke’s Celebrated Criminal Cases of America and gives Packer’s first name as Alfred.
Packer is the subject of Harold Schechter’s true-crime book Man-Eater.

The grill’s slogan was “Have a friend for lunch!”

Bergland said Packer’s life exemplified the spirit and fare of the cafeteria and would “serve all mankind.”
ABC Evening News covered the 1977 plaque event with Barbara Walters.
The strategy succeeded and the cafeteria contracts were terminated soon afterward.

The plaque is now displayed on the wall of the National Press Club’s The Reliable Source members-only bar.
The plaque also serves as a memorial to Stanley Weston, who worked at the USDA and lived from 1931 to 1984.
The National Press Club’s hamburger is called the Alfred Packer Burger.
The comedy musical Cannibal! The Musical was released exclusively in Boulder, Colorado, in 1993 and in the rest of the United States in 1996.
Cannibal! The Musical was Trey Parker’s directorial debut.
Phil Ochs wrote the song “The Ballad of Alferd Packer” in 1964 about the expedition and its aftermath.
Ochs’s use of humor in the song reflects a seemingly lighthearted ongoing attitude toward Packer and his alleged crimes.
The song did not appear on any of Ochs’s studio or live albums.

Packer was originally sentenced to death.
